list.listitem: Acute sialadenitis is clinically diagnosed by the sudden onset of indurated, warm, erythematous swelling of a salivary gland. B

Chronic sialadenitis is less likely to be painful and is characterized by an abnormally firm gland that may be enlarged, normal, or atrophic or can present as symptoms of multiple episodes of acute sialadenitis. C

Acute treatment is by maintenance of adequate hydration and broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy as initial therapy for patients. Obtain aerobic and anaerobic cultures through the duct or by needle aspiration to establish the correct pathogen, especially If treatment fails, surgery is considered or there is an area of fluctuance. B
Application of warm compresses, improving oral hygiene, external or bimanual massage of the gland, sialagogues are often recommended, but data are lacking.

background.definition: Sialadenitis is the inflammation of the salivary glands, including parotid, submandibular, sublingual or minor glands. Acute sialadenitis is less than several weeks, chronic several weeks or more.

list.listitem: Acute sialadenitis rates are largely unknown. One study showed admission rates of 27.5 per million population per year others found it accounts for 0.03% of admissions in US.
Chronic sialadenitis affects 1 in 20,000 individuals.
The incidence of sialadenitis peaks between the 3rd and 6th decades of life.
Rates were not statistically different between genders for diagnosis of sialolithiasis in one study.
Acute sialadenitis is more common in elderly patients with systemic illness or who had a recent surgical procedure, like abdominal surgery or hip replacement surgery.
Chronic sialadenitis has a significant impact on patient's quality of life including changes in activities, chronic symptoms, and effects on the psychosocial domain.
Sialadenitis may be acute, chronic, or acute on chronic and includes multiple causes (see ).
Acute sialadenitis can by caused by obstruction (stenosis, sialolithiasis), injury (post-radiation), infection (bacterial, viral), or a combination of causes.
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common bacterial infection of the glands (see for most common bacterial pathogens).

Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, smoking, renal disease, hypothyroidism, dehydration, malnutrition, immunosuppression, dental infection, neoplasm of oral cavity, tracheostomy, sialectasis, ductal obstruction, prior radiation therapy, I-131 treatment, and Sjögren's syndrome.

Medications that suppress salivary flow predispose to sialadenitis. These include but are not limited to antihistamines, diuretics, antidepressants, neuroleptics, bronchodilators, anxiolytics, antihypertensives, opioids, appetite suppressants, chemotherapy agents, and anticholinergics.
Sialadenitis has been reported as a consequence of iodinated contrast for CT scan as well as radioiodine treatment for thyroid cancer.

Acute sialadenitis is caused by the spread of organisms to the glands by the ascension of oral bacteria through the ducts. Acute obstruction of the gland, such as secondary to a sialolith, may lead to stasis of saliva, inflammation and increased risk of bacterial ascension through the duct (see for full list of bacterial pathogens).
Submandibular glands are obstructed with sialoliths (91%), mucous plugs (3%) and stenosis (6%). In parotid glands, obstruction was due to stenosis (75%), mucous plug (14%) and sialolith (11%).
Another possible route of spread of bacteria is through bacteremia, especially in newborns.
Chronic causes are listed in .
Maintenance of good oral hygiene, adequate hydration, and limiting risk factors including predisposing medications and chronic disease burdens may improve rates, there is no screening available. C
Acute sialadenitis is clinically diagnosed with sudden onset of an indurated, warm, unilateral swelling of the parotid, submandibular, sublingual or minor salivary glands. C
If there is an area of fluctuance, perform needle aspiration and culture for aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. C
Chronic sialadenitis is diagnosed with recurrent symptoms of acute sialadenitis or gland firmness. C

Usually unilateral parotid swelling without tenderness or fever

list.listitem: Acute sialadenitis is characterized by the sudden onset of an indurated, warm, erythematous swelling of salivary glands, usually with purulent drainage at the ductual opening. With parotid involvement, there is swelling of the cheek to the angle of the jaw, whereas with submandibular and sublingual gland involvement, swelling is below the mandible.
Acute sialadenitis may be associated with fever and leukocytosis.
Chronic sialadenitis is characterized by repeated episodes of pain and swelling, often after meals. The glands will be swollen, firm or normal on exam.
Needle aspiration (if acute) or biopsy (if chronic) may be neccessary to guide treatment.
Duct evaluation with radiography, sialography, computer tomography, sialendoscopy is used for recurrent or chronic sialadenitis.

Ultrasound has been shown to be comparable to CT with less radiation, and specific guidelines can be used for diagnosis of different salivary gland disorders. Point-of-care ultrasound may be a bedside option for diagnosing the types of sialadenitis.
Consider sialendoscopy for patients with recurrent sialadenitis (including juvenile recurrent parotitis), and radioiodine induced sialadenitis.
A case series of 49 sialendoscopy procedures on 38 parotid glands and 11 submandibular glands in 29 children found a stone in about half of the latter but none in the parotid glands.
See for a suggested approach to management. of acute symptoms.

In general, treatment of sialadenitis is based on its underlying etiology. Conservative management with maintanance of adequate hydration, pain control with oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medication or acetaminophen, and promptly starting antibiotic therapy if acute bacterial infection is suspected.

Acute antibiotic treatment, pending culture results, includes penicillin plus a beta-lactamase inhibitor, clindamycin or metronidazole plus cefuroxine, ceftriaxone, or, if penicillin-allergic, levofloxacin. A penicillinase-resistant penicillin can also be used. C
MRSA coverage may be needed if the patient is at risk or first-line treatment fails.C
If the patient has systemic symptoms or is not responding to oral antibiotics in 48 hours, admit and start intravenous antibiotics.C
In the event of a well-formed abscess, surgical drainage is necessary.B

Treatment of chronic sialadenitis is focused on control of chronic condition as well as symptom control with hydration, gland massage, warm compresses, sialalogues and antibiotics. Sialendoscopy has been shown to decrease the frequency and severity of episodes.

A penicillinase-resistant penicillin (dicloxacillin 250 mg orally 4 times daily for 10 days), penicillin plus beta-lactamase (amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125mg orally bid for 10 days) is generally adequate as initial outpatient empiric therapy. If penicillin allergic, cephalexin (500mg four times a day for 10 days) if mild allergy, or clindamycin (600mg every 6-8 hours) if severe allergy can be used.

If intravenous therapy is indicated, start with ampicillin-sulbactam (3g every 6 hours) alone or cefuroxime (1.5g every 8 hours), ceftriaxone (1g every 24 hours) or levofloxacin (500mg every 24 hours) plus metronidazole (500mg every 8 hours) or clindamycin (600mg every 6-8 hours)
If MRSA is suspected, use sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, clindamycin, vancomycin, daptomycin or linezolid.
Discontinue antihistamines and other antisialogogic medications whenever possible.

There is very limited evidence regarding oral corticosteroids following sialendoscopy to treat obstructive sialadenitis. A single observational study reported a lower recurrence rate in patients receiving steroids for more than 7 days.
Attempt needle aspiration before surgical intervention due to lower risk of long-term effects. If pus is aspirated in a patient with fever and leukocytosis, surgical drainage is necessary.

Treatment of chronic sialadenitis is focused on control of chronic condition as well as symptom control with hydration, gland massage, warm compresses, sialalogues and antibiotics. Sialendoscopy has been shown to decrease the frequency and severity of episodes.

A case series of 59 patients with chronic sialadenitis due to Sjogren's syndrome or radioactive iodine treatment were managed with sialendoscopy accompanied most commonly by corticosteroid injection and duct dilation, with good results. Most patients had parotid gland involvement. There was no comparison group.
A systematic review found a pooled success rate of 81% for sialadenoscopy for the treatment of obstruction.
Treatment is also directed at reversal of the underlying medical condition responsible.
Application of a warm compress, improving oral hygiene, mouth irrigations, and sialogogues (eg, lemon drops, orange juice) are often recommended, but clinical trial data are lacking.
External or bimanual massage of the gland both intraorally and externally may be employed if the patient can tolerate it, but clinical trials are lacking.
Cannulation and serial dilation of the duct with lacrimal probes can establish ductal patency.
Sialendoscopy is recommended first line intervention for recurrent submandibular and parotid sialadnitis in children.
If the patient does not respond to oral antibiotics within 48 hours, consider hospitalization for IV antibiotics.
Also consider hospitalization for patients who present with abscess and/or systemic symptoms.
Acute bacterial infection can lead to abscess formation and bacterial spread to other structures of the deep neck.
Chronic salivary hypofunction as a result of chronic sialadenitis can lead to difficulty swallowing, taste disorders, dental caries, periodontal disease, oral candidiasis, and poor nutrition.
Sialoendoscopy and lavage resulted in resolution and no recurrence in 93% of children with juvenile recurrent parotitis with a single treatment.
Acute sialadenitis has an excellent prognosis with appropriate treatment of underlying etiology, including antibiotic treatment if indicated.
Chronic sialadenitis depends on medical management of underlying condition.
Consider sialography in the post-treatment phase, as a local salivary gland abnormality was demonstrated in 70% of patients in one series. B
